title: Perimeterless VPC Segmentation and mTLS Guidance for Private Deployments
content:
Purpose:
This doc distills a practical, low-friction approach to running Redwood Private with a "perimeterless" VPC segmentation model, mandatory mTLS between services, hardened firewall rules, RBAC v2 mappings, audit log schema expectations, and a lightweight evidence automation flow for SIEM export. Target audience: SREs, infra engineers onboarding a customer, and security reviewers doing evidence collection for compliance audits.

Goals and constraints:
- Provide deterministic network boundaries that do not rely on a single edge firewall.
- Enforce service-to-service identity via mutual TLS (mTLS) and short-lived certs.
- Map RBAC v2 identities to network policies for least-privilege connectivity.
- Produce audit-log shape and SIEM-ready export with minimal post-processing.
- Offer automated evidence collection that produces tamper-evident bundles for audits.

High-level pattern summary:
1) Micro-segmentation by role: divide the VPC into logical segments (control-plane, model-hosting, telemetry, customer-data, management) using separate subnets and route tables. Not every segment needs a dedicated NAT/Gateway; we prefer explicit egress proxies for telemetry and package fetching.
2) No single "perimeter" ACL: rely on host-level and service-level policies (mTLS + service mesh / sidecar where possible) plus cloud ACLs for coarse controls.
3) mTLS everywhere: service certificates issued from a customer-specific PKI (or Redwood-managed PKI under contract) with automatic rotation and short TTLs (default 6 hours).
4) RBAC v2 -> Network bindings: RBAC role assertions are translated to network policy tags that the dataplane enforces (see mapping example below).

Suggested VPC layout (minimal):
- Subnet A (control-plane): NAT and bastion access controls; only management IPs, cluster control-plane components.
- Subnet B (model-hosting): GPU hosts, autoscaling groups; restrict inbound to load-balancers and specific controller IP ranges.
- Subnet C (telemetry): forwarding to observability stack (e.g., fluentd/ops endpoint); Strict egress controls to SIEM endpoints.
- Subnet D (customer-data): encrypted storage, customer-specific network policies; access only from router components with mTLS roles.
- Subnet E (services): shared stateless services (config, auth, routing), require mTLS and RBAC token checks.

ASCII diagram (logical):

  [Internet LB]
       |
  [Ingress Load Balancer - per-customer route policies]
       |
  +-------------------------------+
  | VPC                         |
  |  +---------+  +-----------+  |
  |  | SubnetB |  | SubnetE   |  |
  |  |(model)  |  |(services) |  |
  |  +----+----+  +--+--------+  |
  |       |          |           |
  |   +---v----------v----+      |
  |   | SubnetD (customer) |     |
  |   +---------------------+    |
  |   +---------------------+    |
  |   | SubnetC (telemetry) |    |
  |   +---------------------+    |
  +-------------------------------+

Key rules and rationale:
- Default-deny at multiple layers: host firewall (iptables/nftables) defaults to DROP for inbound unless mTLS identity verified, and cloud security groups deny intra-subnet by default then allow by tag.
- Explicit egress for telemetry: only the telemetry subnet may egress to external SIEM endpoints; other subnets reach telemetry via internal mTLS endpoints.
- Management plane only from control-plane subnets and customer VPN / Direct Connect with strict MFA and Just-In-Time access.

Firewall rule examples (cloud-neutral pseudo-rules):
- Allow: SubnetE -> SubnetB (TCP 443) IF src has tag role:router AND mTLS identity includes role:model-svc
- Deny: SubnetB -> SubnetD (any) unless mTLS identity role:storage-proxy
- Allow: SubnetC -> External.SIEM (TCP 6514/514) via dedicated egress IPs; TLS with client cert
- Management access: Control-plane CIDR -> All subnets (TCP 22/443/9650) only through bastion set with conditional access

Host-level example (systemd nftables snippet, illustrative):
- Base chain: drop inbound by default
- Allow loopback and established
- Allow TCP 443 if xtxt-based mTLS mark present (set by sidecar after handshake)

mTLS deployment pattern and PKI:
- PKI options: customer-managed CA (preferred for sensitive customers) or Redwood-managed CA with customer-specific intermediate.
- Certs: short-lived leaf certs (Recommended TTL: 6h–12h); keys are ephemeral, stored in memory by sidecars.
- Rotation: automated rotation agent (runs in host namespace) requests new cert pre-expiry and hot-swaps without connection churn where possible.
- Identity assertions: SAN contains role, service-id, deployment-id. The server validates both cert chain and SAN TTL.
- Revocation: CRL is avoided in favor of short TTLs plus an online revocation list in the control plane for urgent removal.

RBAC v2 mapping to network policy (example):
- RBAC Role: model-reader -> grants token scope [model:read], cluster role "model-reader"
- Network tag mapping: model-reader -> net-tag:model-readers
- Enforcement: dataplane checks token + mTLS SAN and allows traffic only if net-tag present on source instance

Example RBAC->Network binding table (plaintext):
- role:admin -> net-tag:admin-mgmt -> allowed: control-plane, all management ports
- role:model-host -> net-tag:model-host -> allowed: model-hosting subnets, metrics pull on 9100
- role:telemetry -> net-tag:telemetry-agent -> allowed: send to telemetry cluster only

Audit log schema (canonical example - keep small and SIEM-friendly):
- All logs SHOULD be structured JSON (one JSON object per line). Minimal fields: timestamp, event_id, actor, actor_role, action, resource, resource_id, src_ip, dst_ip, tls_peer_identity, request_id, outcome, message, raw_metadata_url.

Sample event (as a single-line JSON for SIEM):
{\n  \"timestamp\": \"2026-02-20T18:21:43Z\",\n  \"event_id\": \"evt-9d7c-4231\",\n  \"actor\": \"service:router-1\",\n  \"actor_role\": \"router\",\n  \"action\": \"connect\",\n  \"resource\": \"model-host\",\n  \"resource_id\": \"host-gpu-12\",\n  \"src_ip\": \"10.12.4.23\",\n  \"dst_ip\": \"10.12.8.7\",\n  \"tls_peer_identity\": \"CN=model-svc-1,OU=customer-42,ST=redwood\",\n  \"request_id\": \"req-ffc3\",\n  \"outcome\": \"allowed\",\n  \"message\": \"mTLS validated and RBAC check passed\",\n  \"raw_metadata_url\": \"s3://evidence-bucket/2026-02-20/evt-9d7c-4231.json\"\n}

SIEM export considerations and pipeline:
- Ship structured JSON with newline-delimited objects. Avoid nested complex arrays. Fields must be consistent across components.
- Enrich logs at the telemetry aggregator with: geoip (if external), customer_id (if applicable), and high-level policy_decision (allow/deny/reason).
- Use a dedicated egress IP and TLS client authentication to the SIEM so customer SIEM can whitelist only one IP and require cert-based ingestion.
- Retention: raw evidence objects moved into immutable S3 with object-lock for audit windows (configurable by customer).

Evidence automation: minimal flow for an audit snapshot
1) Trigger: compliance run or ad-hoc request (ticket PD-4821 style).
2) Snapshot collection: telemetry aggregator exports all events for a time window and produces a manifest (ndjson) plus a signed hash manifest.
3) Configuration snapshot: export of firewall rules, routing tables, active RBAC role bindings, PKI intermediate cert fingerprints.
4) Crypto: bundles are signed with infra-key (HSM/KMS) and checksummed (SHA256).
5) Upload: bundles and manifest placed into customer-specific evidence S3 (or requested storage) with object-lock.
6) Delivery: provide a signed link and verification instructions to the auditor.

Automation script checklist (what to run for a standard evidence bundle):
- export-telemetry --start <t0> --end <t1> --out events-<t0>-<t1>.ndjson
- export-firewall --format json > firewall.json
- export-rbac --format yaml > rbac-binding-<date>.yaml
- sign-bundle --private-key ksm://infra/keys/evidence-signing --files events-*.ndjson firewall.json rbac-*.yaml --out evidence-<date>.zip
- upload-evidence --bucket s3://evidence-bucket/customer-42/2026-02-20 --file evidence-<date>.zip --put-lock

Operational hardening checklist (pre-deployment and periodic reviews):
- [ ] Enforce short-lived mTLS certs and automate rotation.
- [ ] Default-deny host firewall and cloud security groups.
- [ ] Map RBAC v2 roles to network tags and validate that tag assignments exist for every role.
- [ ] Configure telemetry egress via a dedicated subnet and restrict external endpoints by TLS client cert.
- [ ] Enable structured JSON logs at the source and validate field presence with a schema validator.
- [ ] Implement evidence automation and run a dry-run export quarterly.
- [ ] Enable object-lock on evidence storage and key-wrapping with customer KMS when requested.
- [ ] Run simulated revocation: issue a revocation action and confirm the short TTL + control-plane revoke list cause access to be denied within the SLA window.
- [ ] Provide a playbook for emergency key rotation and forensic artifacts collection.

Checklist acceptance criteria (examples):
- mTLS Rotation: 90% of cert rotations completed automatically within 5 minutes of predecessor expiry (monitored metric).
- Policy Enforcement: >99.99% of unauthorized connect attempts logged and fed to SIEM within 30s.
- Evidence Availability: automated bundle generation completes < 45 minutes for a 24-hour window.

Implementation notes and gotchas:
- Sidecar approach: easiest to roll out in containerized deployments. For VMs, use host agents that integrate with the local proxy.
- Token vs cert checks: prefer cert-first (mTLS) for initial connection; token introspection for authorization decisions.
- CRL delays: because distributed CRL checks can be slow, short TTLs are the primary protection mechanism. Maintain an emergency revoke list in control-plane for urgent blocks.
- Time sync: ensure all hosts and telemetry agents have NTP within 5s of control-plane to preserve log ordering and signature validity.

Appendix A — Example SIEM field mapping:
- siem.timestamp = timestamp
- siem.user = actor
- siem.role = actor_role
- siem.action = action
- siem.resource = resource/resource_id
- siem.ip_src = src_ip
- siem.ip_dst = dst_ip
- siem.policy_decision = outcome
- siem.evidence_url = raw_metadata_url

Appendix B — Emergency playbook (short):
1) Detect: alert from SIEM -> run live-query on telemetry aggregator for request_id
2) Revoke: issue revoke to control-plane revoke list for affected cert fingerprint
3) Isolate: apply temporary security-group block on affected hosts/subnet
4) Collect: kick off evidence automation for the incident window and mark bundle as "incident"
5) Rotate: rotate affected PKI intermediates if compromise confirmed

Notes and next steps:
- Action item: implement telemetry schema validator in telemetry-agent (owner: Priya Kaur, ticket PD-4890).
- Action item: provide a Terraform module that sets the standard subnets + example security groups and exports config for the evidence automation scripts (owner: Diego Alvarez).
- Review cadence: quarterly review with security + SRE and ad-hoc evidence runs on request.

If you want, I can also produce: a) a compact Terraform example snippet for the recommended security groups, b) a sample telemetry-schema.json file for the validator, or c) a short demo script that produces a signed evidence bundle (bash + aws cli).
